Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave Program Publishes Actuarial Report, First Claims Report

October 1, 2026

For Immediate Release: Oct. 1, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

Actuarial report projects PFML Trust Fund will remain stable for the next 10 years

AUGUSTA - The Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) program has published its second annual actuarial report, as well as its first claims report on Oct. 1, 2026.

PFML became law in 2023 and is a statewide program that provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of paid leave for medical, parental, family care, military family or safe leave.

The PFML program began accepting claims on March 30, 2026, and began paying benefits on May 1, 2026. This initial claims report covers the program's first three months of claims activity, from March 30 through June 30, 2026. Future claims reports will be published annually and will cover a full year of claims activity.

Highlights of the reports include:

  • The PFML Trust Fund remains solvent and based on updated revenue and claim expenditure, is projected to remain stable for the next 10 years.
  • The program received 8,376 applications between March 30 and June 30, 2026.
  • Among the claims approved, medical leave was the most common reason, followed by welcoming a new child and caring for a family member. Other leave reasons represented a very small portion of the overall claim volume.

"We are excited to see the PFML Program effectively off the ground and helping Maine workers and businesses through life's big moments, both now and for years to come," said PFML Director Luke Monahan.

More information on the PFML program, including how to apply, can be found on the program's website: https://www.maine.gov/paidleave/

Employees, employers and self-employed individuals with questions can call 207-621-5024 between8 a.m. and 5 p.m. Monday through Friday. Employees can send a message through the Benefits Application Portal, while employers and self-employed individuals can send a message through the Maine Paid Leave Contributions Portal.

Consistent with the recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the Maine CDC recommends the following respiratory virus immunization for the 2026-2027 season:

  • COVID-19: Vaccination is recommended for

    • children and adolescents ages 2 through 18 years who are at increased risk for severe COVID-19 or who want to be vaccinated;
    • adults age 19 and older;
    • pregnant individuals.

Reminders in Preparation for Maine eCourts and eFiling in Cumberland County Courts

Date: 9/23/2026

On Monday, September 28, 2026, the Maine Judicial Branch is expanding Maine eCourts to all case types in Judicial Region 2, comprising Cumberland County Unified Criminal Docket (UCD), Cumberland County Superior Court, Portland District Court, and Bridgton District Court.

All case types -- civil, family, juvenile and criminal cases -- will be included in the transition from paper filing to electronic filing. As of Monday, September 28, all mandatory electronic filers pursuant to the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS) will be required to eFile documents in these courts. Self-represented litigants (parties who do not have attorneys) who file fewer than six cases in a calendar year will not be required to eFile.

Court Closures and Emergency Filing Procedures
To prepare for the implementation of Maine eCourts and eFiling on September 28, Region 2 courts are currently operating on a modified schedule and have emergency filing procedures in place. In addition, all Region 2 courts will be closed from 8 a.m. to noon the week of September 28th. Please refer to the schedule of closures and emergency procedures during these closings.

ShareFile Discontinued in Region 2 Courts
The ShareFile platform used in Region 2 courts will be disabled for all criminal, civil violation, juvenile filings, and GAL vouchers, at 2:00 p.m. on Thursday, September 24. Starting Monday, September 28, attorneys must instead use eFileMaine. Please note, attorney vouchers filed pursuant to the Standing Order regarding Payment to Court-Appointed Counsel will continue to be accepted by ShareFile for a grace period of 60 days.

Training Resources
For attorneys and staff who are new to using eFileMaine, we highly recommend viewing the recorded videos, particularly the video excerpts, available on the Maine eCourts Trainings and Resources web page. In addition to the recordings, the information and resources available on the Maine eCourts Trainings and Resources web page offer guidance for setting up your eFileMaine account and instructions to eFile documents successfully.

Personal Identifying Information (PII) Attachment (CR-CV-JV-297)
Pursuant to the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS) filers are responsible for omitting or redacting nonpublic information in electronically filed documents. If the filer decides to omit rather than redact, the personal identifying information must be included on this form.

The PII form should be uploaded as an attachment to the associated filing document, in the same way that an exhibit is submitted.

Online Fine Payments
As of September 28th, parties who wish to make criminal fine payments online for cases in Cumberland County will be directed to the new online payment portal, Maine eCourts Criminal Fines and Fees. Visit Maine eCourts: Pay a Court Fine to learn more.

Support
Support for eFiling is available by emailing ecourtshelp@courts.maine.gov or by calling (207) 213-2813, Monday through Thursday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

For more information on Maine eCourts and eFiling, visit: https://www.courts.maine.gov/ecourts/index.html

Welcome to the online digital collection of the Maine State Archives, a bureau within the Department of the Secretary of State. We maintain approximately 8 miles of official state records (both paper and digital) that are deemed permanently valuable. These records include bills introduced in the Legislature, reports from the Governor's Executive Council, election returns, deeds and maps from the Maine Land Office, vital statistics prior to 1892, federal census records up to 1880, county court records dating back to 1636, and military records through World War I, among others.

items.title: Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week - September 28 through October 4
items.content_text:
WHEREAS
, food is one of Maine’s most valuable resources and is essential for the health and nutrition of all our 1.4 million residents; and
WHEREAS
, nearly 40 percent of food produced in Maine is never eaten – over 361,000 tons annually – primarily ending up in landfills where it produces dangerous methane gas which is 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide and a major contributor to climate change; and
WHEREAS
, Maine people can save money by preventing wasted food, with the average Maine family spending nearly $3,000 annually on food that is thrown away; and
WHEREAS
, over 80 percent of consumers misunderstand food date labels causing large amounts of perfectly good food to be thrown away in homes, businesses, and even food pantries; and
WHEREAS
, Maine communities can substantially reduce their waste disposal costs by preventing wasted food since food is the single largest municipal solid waste component; and
WHEREAS
, Maine K-12 schools have a special role in educating our next generation to reduce, recover, and recycle the estimated 7 million pounds of school food wasted annually; and
WHEREAS
, we can help our farmers, strengthen our local food systems, and conserve our natural resources – water, air, energy, and land – by valuing Maine food and composting food scraps instead of wasting it as trash;
NOW THEREFORE
, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim the week of September 28-October 4, 2026, as
Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week
and I encourage all Maine people to become aware of the wasted food in our homes, schools and all around us, and to commit to stop throwing food away.
In testimony whereof, I have caused
the Great Seal of the State to be
hereunto affixed GIVEN under my
hand at Augusta this second day
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

Looking Ahead: Eligibility-Dedicated Data Feed to Support MaineCare Renewals and Enrollment

Sep 04, 2026

Two weeks ago, we announced communications support for MaineCare partners and providers regarding changes the federal government is making to MaineCare (Maine’s Medicaid program) eligibility. This message provides an early look at planned data-sharing that will help the Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) verify information needed for MaineCare eligibility. Our goal is to help eligible Mainers keep their coverage and access to services with as little disruption as possible.

No action is needed now. We are sharing this information early to make providers aware of what is being planned. We will share more information as plans and timelines are finalized.

DHHS will continue to use administrative data sources it has access to as much as possible to support automatic (“passive”) renewals for MaineCare members. Federal changes to eligibility mean we need additional information to help more eligible members maintain their MaineCare coverage. This data will help Mainers continue to benefit from MaineCare, which in turn will help providers minimize the impact of these federal Medicaid cuts on their revenue and on their charity and uncompensated care.

Clinical Data Will Help People Stay Enrolled in MaineCare

Electronic health record (EHR) systems contain clinical data that Maine and numerous other states are planning to use to help exempt Medicaid applicants and members with work-limiting health conditions from Work Requirements. In Maine, this data will support MaineCare eligibility determination activities administered by the Office for Family Independence (OFI). DHHS intends to partner with providers to collect this information through HealthInfoNet, the State’s contractor for this work. HealthInfoNet will identify indicators of exemptions from work requirements by collecting and processing this clinical data from providers. Using clinical data alongside claims and other administrative data to generate more timely and comprehensive information will help keep Mainers enrolled in MaineCare. We will refer to the data sent to HealthInfoNet for this purpose as the eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed.

Until the eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed is established we will be basing automatic exceptions for work-limiting health conditions on claims data alone in order to meet implementation deadlines.

This Data Sharing Will Be Separate from the Health Information Exchange

The eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed will be separate from the health information exchange (HIE) data that many providers already share with HealthInfoNet.

The eligibility-dedicated data feed will include only the information needed to support MaineCare eligibility activities. This information will be stored separately from HIE data. It will not be available through HealthInfoNet’s clinical portal or through analytics tools used by some provider organizations. The eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed will be used only in support of OMS and OFI activities associated with eligibility.

Key details to note:

  • The steps needed for a provider to establish this new data feed will vary by provider organization. For example, some provider organizations already have a data feed with HealthInfoNet that can be used as a starting point. Capabilities of the organization’s EHR vendor or technology support may also affect the work needed to establish the data feed. Providers eligible for relevant Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding may consider using this funding for these costs, as determined by the allowable uses of specific RHTP opportunities.
  • We expect it will take the majority of provider organizations two to four months to build their eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed with HealthInfoNet. This time range will be dependent on provider organization’s or vendor’s availability to engage with HealthInfoNet. We expect it will take less time than building a typical HIE data sharing connection with HealthInfoNet.
  • Clinical care teams are not expected to need to take additional steps to send this information as part of their day-to-day work. Once the data feed is established, the identified data categories will be shared automatically with HealthInfoNet.
  • Broad categories of exemptions in statute for work-limiting health conditions include those who are blind or disabled, have a substance use disorder, disabling mental disorder, or complex medical condition. DHHS continues to work with the federal government to clarify data related to these categories that may assist states to automatically exempt individuals, including information related to a person’s ability to work. Kinds of data may include demographic information, diagnosis indicators, encounter or event indicators, and billing codes, among others.

More Information Will Be Coming – No Action Needed Now The Department and HealthInfoNet will distribute instructions for provider organizations to opt into this initiative and implement the eligibility-dedicated data feed. Future communications will include information such as:

  • Which provider types will be prioritized for establishing these connections
  • How providers can participate
  • The types of information that will be needed
  • Technical requirements and specifications
  • Onboarding and implementation steps
  • Timelines
  • Testing procedures
  • Contacts for technical and operational qu

MEMO

FROM: Barbara Archer Hirsch, Commission Counsel 
Colin R. Hurd, Deputy Commission Counsel 
DATE: July 23, 2025 
RE: Standard of review for right-to-sue requests made before 180 days have passed 
As you are aware, 5 M.R.S. § 4612(6)(B), enacted in 2023, delineates the circumstances 
in which the Executive Director (“ED”) shall issue a right-to-sue letter (“RTS”) to a complainant 
who requests one before their complaint has aged 180 days with the Commission. Prior to the 
2023 enactment, complainants could never request an RTS prior to 180 days. Now, the 
Commission “shall” issue an early RTS when two elements are concurrently met. First, the ED 
must determine that the complainant demonstrated good cause for requesting the RTS before the 
passage of 180 days, and second, the ED must certify that it is probable that the Commission will 
be unable to conclude its investigation before the 180
th day from the date on which the complaint 
was filed. After 180 days have passed, the complainant may request and receive an RTS without 
having to meet these standards.  
The second element of § 4612(6)(B) is relatively straightforward. The first element, 
however, is more nuanced. The Maine Human Rights Act does not define “good cause”. The 
Commission’s Procedural Rule provides that the Commission may grant extensions of certain 
time limits “for good cause shown”, 94-348 C.M.R. Ch. 2, § 2.11(C), but also do not define the 
term.  In practice, the Commission requires that parties seeking extensions demonstrate that the 
requested extension is necessary due to extenuating circumstances, such as serious personal 
illness or a death in the family; inconvenience is insufficient to meet this standard.

items.title: US Department of Labor recovers $732K for 31 workers owed overtime, minimum wages by Florida seafood restaurant
items.content_text: MIAMI – The U.S. Department of Labor has recovered $732,976 for 31 Florida restaurant workers from a Pompano Beach seafood restaurant owner who failed to pay the workers their full wages.Lucky King LLC – operating as Miyako Japanese Buffet – paid most employees a monthly salary between $1,000 to $3,000, even though employees typically worked more than 40 hours per week. The department’s Wage and Hour Division investigators determined the employer also failed to pay minimum wage for all hours worked and maintain required records, all in violation of the Fair Labor Standards Act.Federal recordkeeping regulations require employers to keep records for each employee covered by the FLSA, including identification details, hours worked, and the wages earned.Workers and employers can call the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division. The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the Family and Medical Leave Act. Learn more about the Wage and Hour Division, including a search tool that workers can use if they think they may be owed back wages collected by the division. Download the agency’s free timesheet app for iOS and Android devices to track hours and pay.

items.title: Ovarian Cancer Awareness Month - September
items.content_text:
WHEREAS
, ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer deaths of women in the United States, and it causes more deaths than any other gynecologic cancer; and
WHEREAS
, the American Cancer Society estimates that 21,010 cases of ovarian cancer will be newly diagnosed in 2026 and that 12,450 individuals will die from the disease nationwide, including 100 new cases and 70 deaths in Maine; and
WHEREAS
, many people are unaware of the symptoms of ovarian cancer, which can often include bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, difficulty eating or feeling full quickly, urinary issues, and several more that are easily confused with other diseases; and
WHEREAS
, the lack of an early detection test for ovarian cancer combined with its vague symptoms means that approximately 80 percent of cases of ovarian cancer are detected at an advanced stage; and
WHEREAS
, all women are at risk for ovarian cancer, but approximately 20 percent of women who are diagnosed with ovarian cancer have a hereditary predisposition to the disease which places them at even higher risk; and
WHEREAS
, the family history of a woman has been found to play an important role in accurately assessing their risk of developing ovarian cancer, and medical experts believe that family history should be taken into consideration during the annual well-woman visit of any woman; and
WHEREAS
, ongoing investments in ovarian cancer research and education and awareness efforts are critical to closing these gaps and improving survivorship for women with ovarian cancer;
NOW THEREFORE
, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim September 2026 as
Ovarian Cancer Awareness Month
throughout the State of Maine, and I urge all citizens to recognize this observance.

About the Leave No Trace Spotlight Program

Each year, Leave No Trace selects nominated outdoor areas for its Spotlight program, which brings communities together to care for and protect places people love to visit. Bradbury Mountain State Park, located in Pownal, is one of Maine's original five state parks. The park offers more than 20 miles of trails for hiking, mountain biking, and horseback riding, along with camping and opportunities to experience the area's natural and cultural history. The summit of Bradbury Mountain provides expansive views and is a popular location for observing the annual migration of hawks and other birds of prey. PROCESS FOR APPOINTMENT AS A BAIL COMMISSIONER 
 
Bail Commissioners are appointed by the Chief Judge of the District Court and serve at the pleasure of the 
Court. They must be available to work on an irregular on-call schedule including nights, weekends, and 
holidays. Appointments are made after review of an application, reference calls, a background investigation, 
and a determination by the Chief Judge as to the need for a Bail Commissioner in the area where the applicant 
lives. 
 
Persons who are currently employed by, or have a family member currently employed by, the following 
agencies/businesses, are not eligible to apply: 
• A Law enforcement agency; 
• A Jail/correctional facility; 
• A Law firm; 
• The Department of Corrections; 
• A Prosecutor’s office; 
• A regional communications/dispatch center; and/or 
• A Town/City, County, State, or Federal government agency that has a law enforcement 
agency under its supervision.

• Attend a mandatory training; 
• Pass a fingerprint-based FBI criminal history background check; 
• Complete an online certification to view Criminal Justice Information; 
• Job shadow an experienced bail commissioner; and 
• Open a dedicated bail commissioner bank account.

When Hidden Circle Mobile Home Park in Jay went up for sale, that's exactly what the residents were afraid of: someone hiking up the rent and eventually pushing people out of their homes.

According to the 2024 data, nearly 10 percent of Maine people live in manufactured housing, including mobile home communities. Forty-five thousand people in Maine live in a mobile home park. Out-of-state companies have started buying up some of Maine's mobile home parks and then significantly raising rents, in some cases as high as 50 percent. 

And rent increases don't necessarily mean nicer parks either, no improvements necessarily. Corporations know that residents can't easily pick up their home and move it elsewhere, no matter how much the company neglects the park. As one resident in Jay said, "At one time, the park used to look nice. Now they've stopped that, and yet they have increased our rent. If this continues to have higher lot rent payments, then I'm not going to be able to live where I am."

The buying up of mobile home parks by out-of-state entities is a nationwide trend, but here in Maine, we're doing something about it. Last year, we enacted the "Right of First Refusal" law, which requires that residents of a mobile home park be given a chance to purchase their park if they can put together a matching offer when it's put up for sale. That measure strengthened our 2023 "Opportunity to Purchase" law, which required that residents of a mobile home park be allowed to present a competitive offer to buy their park if it's put up for sale.

Well, earlier this week, I visited Jay to celebrate the first residents to take advantage of our new "Right of First Refusal" law to purchase their park, instead of being left to the whims of an out-of-state buyer. Hidden Circle is now the 14th resident-owned manufactured home community in Maine. Resident-owned—isn't that great?

In addition to financing from the Genesis Fund and Maine Community Foundation, Hidden Circle Mobile Home Community was able to make the $1 million purchase to protect these 31 lots with $310,000 as well from our Mobile Home Park Preservation Fund.

My Administration and the Legislature dedicated $8 million in total in recent years to MaineHousing to create this Mobile Home Park Preservation Fund to assist residents in purchasing their own mobile home parks. With that funding, more than 900 homes are expected to be preserved across six parks from Brunswick to Bangor, Turner to Saco.

Last month, nation-leading laws to further protect mobile home park residents took effect in Maine, including laws to limit rent increases, laws to make it easier to expand mobile home parks, and laws creating a way for mobile homeowners to obtain a mortgage—and that could save them hundreds of dollars every month in housing costs.

I was proud to sign those bills into law earlier this year to protect residents in Jay and other towns across Maine from predatory, out-of-state companies. Now, the residents of Hidden Circle Park in Jay have control over how much rent to charge and how that money will be spent. They have control over their common infrastructure, and they can make improvements as they see fit.

Well, we still have a lot more work to do to protect Maine people and mobile home parks from being exploited by companies who simply want to use them to extract a profit, but I am proud of how we worked together with the Legislature to preserve this vital form of housing for people in Maine.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.
